content.text:
Happy to go deeper on both — these are the two most conceptually interesting of the six, and neither is "just change a line."

## #4 — The redundant re-run on locale change

### What that effect is actually for

The preview page is built in **two phases**, split across two components:

- **Phase 1 — `ContentfulPreviewPage`:** *"What kind of thing is this entry?"* It calls `client.getEntry(entryId)`, reads `entry.sys.contentType.sys.id` (e.g. `collectionPageExp`), and stashes it in `experienceTypeId` state. This phase exists only because the `/preview` route is meant to work for **any** Experience content type — it has to discover the type before it can fetch properly.
- **Phase 2 — `ExperienceView`:** *"Now fetch and render that experience."* It calls `useFetchById({ id, experienceTypeId, localeCode: locale })`. **This is the phase where locale actually matters** — it's the localized content fetch.

So `locale` legitimately belongs to Phase 2. Phase 1's job — figuring out the *type* — has nothing to do with language.

### Why locale is provably irrelevant to Phase 1

A Contentful entry has **exactly one content type across all locales** — the content type lives in `sys` (structural metadata), not in the localized field values. It is structurally impossible for `entry.sys.contentType.sys.id` to differ between `en-AU` and `fr`. And note the call itself: `client.getEntry(entryId)` — **no locale argument is passed**. So the value Phase 1 extracts is identical regardless of locale.

### What React actually does when `locale` is in the deps

When the language changes, here's the cascade (`contentfulPreview/index.tsx:98-117`):

1. `ContentfulPreviewPage` re-renders (the `locale` prop changed).
2. `locale` is in the dep array → React tears down the old effect (`active = false`, abandoning any in-flight lookup) and **re-runs it**.
3. First thing the new run does: `setExperienceTypeId(null)` (line 101). **That wipes the known type.**
4. With the type wiped, the render falls into `if (!experienceTypeId) return <Spinner/>` → **the whole preview blanks to a spinner.**
5. `getEntry(entryId)` fires again over the network → returns the **same** content type.
6. `setExperienceTypeId(sameValue)` → re-render → Phase 2 resumes.

So you pay a network round-trip **and** a full-screen spinner blank to re-derive a fact that cannot have changed.

### The reassurance (this is the part worth internalizing)

The natural worry is: *"If I remove `locale`, won't the preview stop updating when the editor switches language?"* **No** — because the locale-dependent fetch lives in **Phase 2**, and Phase 2 keeps its own locale reactivity: `ExperienceView`'s `useFetchById({ ..., localeCode: locale })` re-fetches the localized content whenever locale changes, all on its own. Removing `locale` from Phase 1 doesn't remove any locale responsiveness — it just stops the redundant *type* re-lookup sitting on top of it.

So removing it is:
- **Safe** — the value isn't used inside the effect, and the fact it fetches is locale-invariant.
- **Actually better UX** — on language switch, Phase 1 now does nothing (no blank), and Phase 2 smoothly swaps in the localized content.

### Why it's here, and why nothing flags it

It's a very natural "the component uses `locale`, so I'll add it to the deps" reflex. Normally `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` is the thing that would comment ("unnecessary dependency: 'locale'") — but this repo deliberately turns `exhaustive-deps` **off** (replaced by `use-effect-no-deps`). So there's no automated nag; it's a human-judgment catch, which is exactly why CodeRabbit filed it as a *nitpick*, not an error. **Fix stays a one-liner:** `[client, entryId, locale]` → `[client, entryId]`.

---

## #6 — Lint is a *checker*, not a *gate*

### The core distinction

There are two different things people lump together as "we have linting":

- A **checker** = the tool + rules exist and *can* find problems. ✅ This repo has that: ESLint is configured, `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` is set to `error`, the plugin is installed, and `npm run lint` works.
- A **gate** = the checker runs **at a checkpoint that can block bad code from progressing**. ❌ This repo has *no* gate.

A checker with no gate is a smoke alarm with no battery. It'll happily detect the fire — if someone walks over and presses the test button by hand. Nothing goes off on its own.

### Where the checkpoints are, and why neither fires

There are exactly two places a lint gate can live, and both are empty:

| Checkpoint | Blocks | Status here |
|---|---|---|
| **pre-commit hook** (`scripts/hooks/pre-commit`) | the commit, locally | No lint step — verified |
| **CI required check** (`.github/workflows/qa.yml`) | the merge | No lint job anywhere — verified |

`npm run lint` exists as a script, so a disciplined dev *can* run it — but "can, if they remember" is not enforcement.

### Why this is the worst bug-class to leave unguarded

Look at what the *other* green checks actually prove, and what they miss:

- TypeScript compiled ✅ — but a Rules-of-Hooks violation is **type-valid**; `tsc` can't see it.
- Vitest / Storybook / Playwright passed ✅ — but a hooks violation is a **runtime fragility that only throws on a specific render/navigation sequence** (recall: `?preview` toggling on a token-absent env). None of those suites happened to hit that sequence.

Static lint (`react-hooks/rules-of-hooks`) is the **one tool designed to catch it deterministically** — and it's the one tool not running. So the safety net with the biggest hole is precisely the one meant to catch the scariest, least-visible failure.

### The proof, as a narrative

- Commit `4a11982` was on the PR, deployed to dev, and human-reviewed. I piped its `experience/index.tsx` through the repo's *own* ESLint → **`105:20 error React Hook "useMemo" is called conditionally … react-hooks/rules-of-hooks`**.
- Every CI check on that commit was **green** — because CI never runs lint.
- The only reason it was caught: **you** kept triggering CodeRabbit, and its 06:22 pass flagged it Critical. That's an AI reviewer — non-blocking, non-deterministic, dependent on someone triggering and reading it. Not a gate.
- `bf81428` then fixed it (I confirmed the error is gone).

Swap out one variable — you get busy, don't re-trigger CodeRabbit — and that violation merges to `develop` with a full-green checkmark. That's the actual exposure.

### The fix — deeper than "add a lint job"

Three things a lead should know before handing this to Integration:

1. **Where to put it — and the tradeoff.**
   - *Pre-commit* = fastest feedback (catches it before it's even a commit), but bypassable (`--no-verify`) and only protects devs who installed the hook.
   - *CI job in `qa.yml`* = can't be bypassed, protects everyone, blocks the merge — this is the **real** gate. Ideally both (pre-commit for speed, CI for enforcement).

2. **A job alone doesn't gate — it has to be a *required* check.** Adding a lint job to `qa.yml` only makes lint *visible*. It blocks merges only once it's marked **required in branch-protection settings**. "Add the job" + "require it" = the actual gate. Miss the second half and you've built the alarm but still not wired the bell.

3. **Sequencing matters or you'll block the whole team.** If Integration flips lint to a required gate *today*, the ~100 existing `prettier/prettier` errors in this PR (and likely other in-flight branches) go red instantly. Correct rollout: **repo-wide `lint:fix` / clean up existing violations first, *then* turn the gate on.** Otherwise the first thing the new gate does is block everyone's open work.

**Ownership:** both `.github/workflows/qa.yml` and `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` are **Tier 1, Integration-owned (#integration)** — so this is a governance change Integration makes, not something Mani (or a feature branch) can add. Your action as lead: raise it on the PR thread with `4a11982` as the concrete exhibit, and propose the CI lint job + the sequencing above. The lift is ~10 lines of YAML against a script that already exists — cheap insurance for an entire bug class.

- Pickaxe for `"lint"` across the **entire history** of `scripts/hooks/pre-commit` → **zero**. That hook guards Contentful-registry drift and derived-file edits; it has never linted.

That's exactly why it looks like a regression: the surrounding scaffolding is elaborate, so the eye assumes lint rode along with it. It didn't.

It reframes the ask from *"restore a lint gate that broke"* to *"add a lint gate that was never there"* — net-new hardening, no regression hunt, no blame. aiTitle: Investigate closed PR #41 and deployment to dev

content.text:
Genuinely worth separating two things here, because the evidence points in opposite directions for each — and the distinction is the whole answer.

## There *is* a deliberate non-gating philosophy — but it was written for the advisory tools

This part is clearly intentional, documented, and coherent. Commit `8e710d6` (dropping the pre-push CodeRabbit hook) spells out the stance:

> "Same non-gating stance as before: **advisory only, the real gate stays the GitHub PR review.**"

And AGENTS.md step 4 codifies it:

> "The review itself is **still advisory relative to the actual merge gate (the GitHub PR review remains the real gate)**."

So Tim/Mani deliberately chose an architecture where **the human GitHub PR review + CODEOWNERS/branch-protection is the real gate**, and the *mechanical* enforcement they wired is **CodeRabbit + `.coderabbit/ast-grep-rules/` + `semgrep.yml` at PR time** (that's what components.md calls "mechanically enforced" for a11y, and what css.md points to). They even pulled CodeRabbit *out* of git hooks on purpose. That's a real, consistent decision — and for subjective/LLM-style checks it's a defensible one.

## But ESLint-in-CI being absent reads as an oversight, not that decision

Here's the tell. The leads' own Tier-1 rules doc, components.md:56-59, says the complexity rule is:

> "not currently ESLint-enforced … treat this as a self-check … **not something the build will fail on yet**. If this keeps being a problem, **adding those two ESLint rules is a cheap follow-up**."

Read that carefully: it's written on the assumption that **the build *does* fail on configured ESLint rules** — the only reason complexity "won't fail the build" is that it *isn't configured* in `.eslintrc.js`. But we proved the build runs ESLint *nowhere* — so it wouldn't fail on `rules-of-hooks` (which *is* configured as `error`) either. **The governance doc contradicts the actual setup.** A deliberate "we chose not to gate lint" decision wouldn't coexist with a Tier-1 doc that assumes the build enforces lint. So this specific gap looks unexamined — it rode along invisibly, probably under the belief that CI already ran `npm run lint`.

(Corroborating, lightly: `.docs/prompts/omsIntClaudeCodePrompt.md` lists "lint" as a required status check — so the *pattern* of lint-as-CI-gate is in the team's vocabulary; it just wasn't wired into this repo's `qa.yml`. That's a reference/OMS-integration prompt, not this repo's CI spec, so I wouldn't lean on it hard.)

## Why the distinction matters for how you raise it

The non-gating philosophy is sound for **subjective** checks — CodeRabbit's LLM findings, complexity heuristics — where you *want* human judgment at PR time and false positives make a hard gate annoying. But `react-hooks/rules-of-hooks` is the opposite kind of rule: **deterministic, binary, effectively zero false positives, and it catches runtime crashes** invisible to types and tests. That's exactly what you normally *do* gate. It looks like it landed on the "advisory" side of their line by omission, not because anyone weighed it and put it there.

So this isn't a "you got CI wrong" conversation with Tim/Mani — their advisory-vs-gate split is intentional and mostly right. The precise question to put to them is:

> "Was leaving a *deterministic correctness* rule like `rules-of-hooks` ungated a deliberate call, or did it ride along with the (correct) decision to keep the *advisory* tools non-gating? — because components.md reads as if the build already enforces configured ESLint rules, and it doesn't run them anywhere."

I can't read their intent, so I won't assert it — but that's now a 30-second confirmation for you rather than a debate, and you've got the exact doc line (`components.md:59`) and the exact commit (`8e710d6`) that frame both sides. If they say "deliberate," the fix is just correcting components.md's wording so it stops implying a gate that doesn't exist. If they say "oversight," it's the small `qa.yml` lint job.

message.content: for the "Should-fix — drop locale from useEffect deps item" - how essential is it to address this item? if not addressed, what is the implication?

content.text:
Short answer: **low essentiality — it's a pure micro-optimization, not a correctness or security issue.** Safe to defer or skip. Here's the precise reasoning.

## What the dep actually does

`contentfulPreview/index.tsx:98-117` — the effect resolves the entry's *content type* so `ExperienceView` can then fetch it:

```tsx
useEffect(() => {
    if (!client || !entryId) return
    setExperienceTypeId(null)          // ← resets → triggers the spinner
    setTypeError(null)
    client.getEntry(entryId).then(entry => setExperienceTypeId(entry.sys.contentType.sys.id)) …
}, [client, entryId, locale])          // ← locale is never read inside the effect
```

`locale` isn't used anywhere in the effect body. An entry's content type is **locale-invariant** — `getEntry(entryId).sys.contentType.sys.id` returns the same value regardless of locale. So `locale` is an extraneous dependency.

## Implication if not addressed

Only one thing happens, and only in one situation: **if `locale` changes while the `/preview` page stays mounted** (e.g. an editor switches locale in the Studio preview panel via a client-side query change), the effect needlessly re-runs, causing:

1. A brief **loading-spinner flash** — `setExperienceTypeId(null)` re-triggers the `if (!experienceTypeId) return <Spinner>` branch until `getEntry` resolves again.
2. **One redundant `getEntry` API call** to Contentful's Preview API.

That's the entire cost. It resolves to the *same* content type, and locale changes still correctly update the displayed content — because the downstream `ExperienceView` / `useFetchById` reacts to the `locale` prop independently. No wrong data, no crash, no stale render (the `active` guard already handles any race).

## Why it's low-priority

- **Correctness:** none affected — it's wasted work, not wrong work.
- **Blast radius:** `/preview` only — editor-facing, dev/test/sit/uat, **never production, zero customer impact.**
- **May not even fire:** if Studio reloads the iframe on a locale switch (full remount) rather than a client-side query change, the effect re-runs on mount anyway and the extraneous dep never triggers. The flash only appears in the SPA-style-update case.
- **Not lint-caught either way:** this repo disables `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps`, so nothing flags it mechanically — it's a manual nit CodeRabbit raised.

## Recommendation

Do it **only because Mani is already in this file** for the other fixes — it's a literal one-token change (`[client, entryId, locale]` → `[client, entryId]`), zero risk, and it removes a real "why is this here?" smell that CodeRabbit will keep re-flagging. If he *weren't* touching the file, it would not be worth a dedicated commit. So: bundle it, don't prioritize it — and it's not remotely a merge blocker.

**1. The `?preview` no-token path is a three-way mismatch between the two preview routes and the doc.**
CodeRabbit flagged that `.docs/integration/02-contentful.md` still says `?preview` Experience pages "fall back to Delivery API mode" with no token, and it's right that the code no longer does that. Its sibling `/preview` route handles the same no-token condition properly — `res.status(404)` + `noindex` (`contentfulPreview/index.tsx` L168–179). So the two preview entry points disagree, and on prod (where the CPA token is deliberately absent) `/<real-slug>?preview` becomes an indexable 200 — the missing half of the `noindex` gate from my #41 review. The doc compounds it: §9 (L128) even asserts "Both preview paths are `noindex`," which the code currently contradicts.

The **BrowserStack E2E** check is red, but I pulled the log and it isn't your code — `browserstack-node-sdk` crashes at init with "Config file does not exist," before any test runs. Root cause is infra: the SDK is unpinned (npx installs latest each run) and the workflow never sets `BROWSERSTACK_CONFIG_FILE`, so the newer SDK no longer finds the `.browserstack.yml` dotfile. The fix lives in Tier 1 `qa.yml` / `.browserstack.yml` (Integration), and your PR touches none of it — this almost certainly breaks every keyed develop PR right now.
